<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: The Defense Production Act is a 75-year-old bipartisan law that has helped our nation respond to war, natural disasters, and the COVID-19 pandemic. It was created to protect the American people in times of crisis, not to be misused for alternative political agendas or personal gain. Committee Democrats have worked across the aisle to put forward a stronger DPA that modernizes the law, reinforces clear guardrails, and ensures that it remains a tool for the public's good and not abused. This bill, which passed HFSC markup with a vote of 41-0, reauthorizes the Defense Production Act (DPA) of 1950 until 2031. The bill also modernizes and reorganizes DPA for structural clarity and improved oversight.
Background: Per the DPA's Declaration of Policy, ``the security of the United States is dependent on the ability of the domestic industrial base to supply materials and services for the national defense and to prepare for and respond to military conflicts, natural or man-caused disasters, or acts of terrorism within the United States.''\1\ Accordingly, the DPA ``provides the President with an array of authorities to shape national defense preparedness programs and to take appropriate steps to maintain and enhance the domestic industrial base.''\2\
\1\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4502(a)(1).
\2\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4502(a)(4).
Modeled after laws from World War II--particularly the War Powers Acts of 1941 (P.L. 77-354) and 1942 (P.L. 77-507), Congress enacted the DPA\3\ in September 1950 to enable President Harry S. Truman to respond to the industrial requirements of the Korean War. Due to the broad economic powers that the law conferred upon the President, this legislation fell under the sole jurisdiction of the House and Senate Committees on Banking and Currency (now the House Committee on Financial Services and the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs).\4\ As the Korean War ended in 1953, Congress allowed four DPA Titles to lapse, leaving only Title I (``Priorities and Allocations''), Title III (``Expansion of Productive Capacity and Supply''), and Title VII (``General Provisions'') in effect. Congress must periodically reauthorize most of the statute's provisions, although some parts, including a provision in Title VII that governs the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), are permanent. Congress has re-authorized and amended the DPA dozens of times, and the DPA's current authorization expires in September 2026.
\3\P.L. 81-774.
\4\CRS, The Defense Production Act of 1950: History, Authorities, and Considerations for Congress (Oct. 6, 2023).
Title I. ``Priorities and Allocations''--Title I authorizes the President to compel persons, including businesses, to perform and prioritize contracts or orders determined necessary for the national defense,\5\ helping to ensure the availability of scarce resources.\6\ The statute allows the U.S. government to place priority ratings and required delivery dates on individual contracts and purchase orders, including subcontracts and orders performed by entities down a contractor's supply chain.\7\
\5\Ibid, note 5.
\6\See, for example, Senate Committee on Banking and Currency, ``Hearings on the S. 3936,'' July 24-26, 1950 (Washington, D.C.: Government Printing Office, 1950), p. 91. Allocation actions are governed by 15 CFR Sec. 700.30-36.
\7\Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security, Defense Priorities and Allocations System Program (DPAS) (2020).
This authority, which allows a president to tell a private company that it must support U.S. national defense needs above all others, including existing contracts with other governments and private-sector firms, is significant and carries substantial impact. As seen in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, for example, the Department of Commerce extended its priority rating to critical infrastructure, allowing an owner/ operator to expedite the delivery of power generators and transfer switches needed to restore railroad operations around New Orleans.\8\ President Biden invoked Title I authorities to help Baxter International re-open its IV solutions and dialysis products manufacturing facility after Hurricane Helene caused damage that created a national shortage of those essential products.\9\ In some cases, however, the target of the priority rating pushes back. During the COVID-19 pandemic, 3M argued that President Trump's pandemic-era Title I classification towards its firm, forcing it to divert its global production of high-quality face masks to the U.S., would cause a decrease in the production of masks due to retaliatory trade measures by countries down its supply chain.\10\
\8\Virginia Department of Emergency Management, Overview And Application Of The Defense Production Act (Accessed Jun. 11, 2025).
\9\Scripps News, J. Boggs, Biden administration invokes Defense Production Act amid IV shortage caused by hurricane (Oct. 16, 2024).
\10\CNBC, K. Breuninger, 3M warns Trump: Halting exports under Defense Production Act would reduce number of masks available to US (Apr. 3, 2020).
Ultimately, the U.S. government and 3M settled their differences,\11\ but the dispute points to the unintended consequences of this extraordinary authority and the possible legal action that could occur if deployed in an irresponsible and illegal manner. There are examples, too, of the U.S. government exercising its Title I authority without deconflicting with another government, triggering diplomatic concern and, possibly, retaliatory action. Last month, the Trump Administration's standoff with the Trump Administration and Anthropic has caused concern regarding DPA.\12\ The Department of Defense attempted to require Anthropic to use its AI tools to conduct mass domestic surveillance and to create fully autonomous weapons.\13\ Having refused, President Trump threatened to both label Anthropic a ``supply chain risk'' (under Title 10) and label it ``critical'' to the national defense, under DPA, allowing the government to force the company to act at the government's direction. Ultimately, the Trump Administration chose the first option, directing all federal agencies to immediately stop using Anthropic's AI tools.\14\ Whether the DPA threat re-appears against Anthropic or another firm is unknown, but it's clear that the President sees the law as a cudgel with which he can bend companies to his will.
\11\CNN, S. Westwood, J. Diamond, Trump announces face mask manufacturing deal with 3M after contentious negotiations (Apr. 7, 2020).
\12\Brendan Bordelon, `Attempted corporate murder': Trump's threats against Anthropic chill AI industry, Politico (Feb. 27, 2026).
\13\Anthropic, Statement from Dario Amodei on our discussions with the Department of War (Feb 26, 2026).
\14\Brendan Bordelon, `Attempted corporate murder': Trump's threats against Anthropic chill AI industry, Politico (Feb. 27, 2026).
To advise the President on the effective use of DPA authorities, the statute established the Defense Production Act Committee (DPAC), comprised of agency heads and other senior government leaders.\15\ Led by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA),\16\ the DPAC chair's current role is not to direct the actions of the individual member agencies, but to coordinate among the agencies to expedite the supply of and expand the productive capacity for materials and services essential to the national defense.\17\
\15\E-mail correspondence from CRS to House Financial Services Committee minority staff (Feb. 29, 2024).
\16\See 50 U.S.C. 4567, The Chairperson of the DPAC, ``shall be the head of the agency to which the President has delegated primary responsibility for government-wide coordination of the authorities in this chapter.''
\17\FEMA, The Defense Production Act Committee Report to Congress: Calendar Year 2020 (Sep. 20, 2021).
Title III. ``Expansion of Productive Capacity and Supply''--Title III allows the President to expand the production and supply of critical materials and goods\18\ via loans, loan guarantees, direct purchases, and purchase commitments to eligible businesses (i.e., those that meet the definition of domestic sources). That can include the creation or improvements to facilities and initiatives to address skilled workforce shortages in critical industries. Notably, the U.K. and Australia were added to the definition of domestic sources in the FY24 NDAA but while even though these countries are considered domestic sources, the President must first look to the U.S. and Canada as a primary source of production, and only if such a source is not possible, are they able to look to these allies.\19\ Title III activities are paid for by DPA Fund appropriations almost exclusively via grants. Appropriations generally remain available to the executive until expended, but per the current statute, the fund's unobligated balance at the end of each fiscal year may not exceed $750 million.\20\
\18\Projects under Title III include investments in ``select kinetic capabilities, microelectronics, castings and forgings, critical materials, and batteries and energy storage,'' per Assistant Secretary of Defense, Defense Production Act Title III (2024).
\19\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4552.
\20\Ibid. Supra, page 1, note 5.
Title VII. ``General Provisions''--Title VII contains provisions pertaining to the DPA as a whole, including key definitions. It also authorizes the National Defense Executive Reserves (NDER), which establishes of a pool of volunteer executives who could be called to public service in the name of national defense, and DPA voluntary agreements, which bring together business and government to collaborate on solving vexing problems that impact the national defense.\21\ Examples include a recently expired pandemic-era voluntary agreement to enhance coordination and cooperation related to critical healthcare resources\22\ and a series of newer ones focused on nuclear energy technologies.\23\
\21\DefenseOne, J. McGinn, D. Kaniewski, Where Does the Defense Production Act Go from Here? (Nov. 24, 2020).
\22\FEMA, Voluntary Agreement With Private Industry To Respond To Pandemics (Jan. 15, 2021).
\23\The White House, Reinvigorating The Nuclear Industrial Base (May 23, 2025).
``National Defense'' and the Scope of DPA--DPA activities are shaped by the definition of the term national defense, a term that has changed significantly since the law's enactment. In 1992, the term was defined as, ``programs for military and energy production or construction, military assistance to any foreign nation, stockpiling, space, and any directly related activity.''\24\ In 1994, however, emergency preparedness was added to this definition, and in 2003, ``critical infrastructure protection and restoration'' was included. In 2009, P.L. 11-67 added ``critical infrastructure assistance to any foreign nation'' and ``homeland security'' to the definition.\25\
\24\GovInfo, Code of Federal Regulations Title 10--Energy (Jan. 1, 2023).
\25\See ``Amendments'' section of 50 U.S.C. Sec. 4552.
This definition is critical to how the law can be applied. For example, in light of growing competition with China, Title III has been a significant tool to address aggressive and often illegal Chinese economic practices\26\ and has received strong bipartisan support for investments in areas such as critical minerals, rare-earth processing, batteries, magnets, and microelectronics.\27\ It has been used to refill stocks of supplies after the U.S. has distributed weapons to allies like Ukraine.\28\ In June 2022, the Biden Administration issued multiple Presidential Determinations (PDs) allowing the Department of Energy to execute Title III projects relating to renewable energy, ``to lower energy costs for families, reduce risks to our power grid, and tackle the urgent crisis of a changing climate.''\29\ While the Trump Administration has reversed these PDs,\30\ a future president could choose to refocus the application of the law on such technologies.
